title: Intros and interview format
gist: Maya and Priya introduce themselves, Sam joins from Lisbon at 9 p.m. local time, and Maya lays out the 45-minute agenda.

turns.t: Hey, Sam? Can you hear me okay?
Yeah, I can hear you. Hi. Hopefully the video's okay, my connection's been a little weird today, my neighbor is, I think, renovating the entire building.
No, you look great. Well, you look fine, I mean the video looks great. Priya should be jumping on any second, she was coming out of another call that I think ran over.
No worries at all.
So you're in Lisbon, right? What time is it there right now?
It's nine p.m. So, you know, I've had dinner, I've had a coffee, which was probably a mistake, but I'm wide awake. Very awake.
Sorry about that, we tried to find something earlier in your day and it just, the calendar did not cooperate this week.
Honestly it's fine. It's actually kind of a useful data point for both of us, right? Like, this is what the overlap actually looks like in practice.
Hi, sorry, sorry. Hi Sam, I'm Priya.
Hi Priya, nice to meet you.

Perfect timing. Okay so let me just do the quick framing and then we'll get into it. I'm Maya, I'm the engineering manager for the routing team at Tandem, which, despite the name, ends up owning a lot of stuff, including the driver app and the dispatcher dashboard on the frontend side. Priya leads design, so she works across all of that, and she's the person you'd be working with most closely on the design side. Today's about forty-five minutes. I'd like to spend the first chunk on your background, then go pretty deep on one technical area, I'm guessing offline sync because it's kind of all over your resume. Priya's going to ask about how you work with design. Then we'll do a small design problem, nothing with a whiteboard, no coding, just talking it through like we would on a real team. And then I want to save ten minutes or so for your questions, which, honestly, is the part I care about too. Sound good?
Sounds great, yeah.
And just so you know, we're recording this with Sounding, so we can take fewer notes and actually pay attention to you. Hannah mentioned that, I think?
Yeah, she did, that's totally fine.

title: Sam's background: fintech, offline-first app, TypeScript migration
gist: Sam describes five years at fintech Pagora, tech-leading an offline-first React Native app for field agents and a 14-month JavaScript-to-TypeScript migration across 300k lines that cut type-related incidents from about a quarter to under 10%.

turns.t: Cool. So, give us the short version. Who are you, how'd you end up where you are.

Okay, short version. I'm Sam, I'm a frontend engineer, mostly React and React Native for the last, I guess, seven years total. I grew up outside Porto, studied computer science there, did a couple of years at an agency building, you know, marketing sites and the occasional e-commerce thing, which taught me a lot about shipping fast and very little about maintaining anything. And then I joined a fintech called Pagora, which is where I've been for the last five years. Pagora does small business lending, and a big part of the business is field agents, so people who go out and sign up small merchants, like shops, market stalls, that kind of thing, and then go back and collect repayments. A lot of them are in rural Portugal and in Mozambique, where the connectivity is, let's say, aspirational. So I ended up becoming kind of the offline person, which I didn't plan, but here we are.
Aspirational, I like that. So that app, the field agent app, that was React Native from the start?

It was React Native from the start but it was not offline-first from the start, which is kind of the whole story. When I joined it was a pretty standard app, you know, every screen fetched from the API, and if you didn't have a connection you got a spinner and then an error toast. And the agents just, they worked around it. They'd write things on paper and then type them in at night when they got back to wifi at a café or wherever. Which meant the data was a day late, and half the time there were typos, and the credit team hated it. So about a year in, me and one other engineer pitched rebuilding the data layer so the app worked offline by default. Local database on the device, every write goes to the local store first, and then there's a sync engine that pushes and pulls in the background. It took, honestly, longer than we said. We said four months, it was more like seven. But by the end, agents could do a full day with no signal and sync when they got back, and the paper went away, which was the real metric. The paper going away.
How big was the team on that?

On the mobile side we were three, at the peak four. Plus one backend engineer who was more or less dedicated to the sync endpoints, which was important. I don't think you can do this well if the sync protocol is designed only from one side. Like, if the backend just gives you REST endpoints and says good luck, you end up building a really fragile thing on the client.
Yeah. Agreed. And you were, were you leading that, or —

I was the tech lead on it, yeah. Not a manager, I've never managed people, but I wrote the design doc and I made most of the calls on the sync model, and I made some bad ones, which we'll probably get to. I also did a lot of the unglamorous stuff, like the rollout. We had about four hundred agents with the old app, some of them with unsent drafts sitting on their phones, so we couldn't just flip a switch. We shipped it behind a flag, region by region, starting with the agents closest to the office so we could literally drive over if something broke.
We will definitely get to those. Before we do, the TypeScript thing. Three hundred thousand lines is a lot of lines. Tell me about that.

Yeah, so, that was a different kind of project. Less fun, honestly more impactful. So by year three we had, across the mobile app and the agent web portal and a shared package, about three hundred thousand lines of JavaScript. Some Flow annotations in places, which, you know, Flow. And we were having a lot of bugs that were just shape bugs. Something's undefined, something's a string instead of a number, the API changed a field name and nobody noticed for a week. So I pushed for moving to TypeScript and ended up leading it. The way we did it, we didn't do a big bang. We turned on allowJs, so JS and TS could live together, we added a lint rule that said no new JS files, period, and then we migrated bottom-up. Shared utilities and the API client first, because everything depends on those, so typing them gave you the most value per line. Then the data layer, then screens. We used Airbnb's ts-migrate for the first pass on some of the bigger directories, which gets you to compiling but with a lot of any. And then we had a little dashboard that tracked percent of files converted and the count of explicit anys, and we posted it in the channel every Friday. Kind of silly, but people liked watching the number go down.
The Friday number, I love that.
It worked weirdly well. People would sneak in an extra file on Thursday afternoon so their team looked good.
How long did it take, end to end?

About fourteen months to get to fully TypeScript, and then strict mode was another, I want to say, three months after that. We did strict per directory, with a tsconfig that extended the base one, so the newer code was strict before the old stuff was. Which meant for a while you had two sets of rules depending on which folder you were in, which people complained about, but it let us move without stopping feature work.
And did it actually move the bug numbers? Or was it more of a, you know, developer happiness thing.

Both, but I can give you a real number. We tagged production incidents by root cause, and the type-related category, so undefined access, wrong shape, that kind of thing, went from roughly a quarter of our mobile incidents to under ten percent. I don't want to oversell that, part of it was also that we added contract tests on the API at the same time. So it's not all TypeScript. But it was a big part of it.
That's a really honest answer, thank you. Most people just tell me it cut bugs by eighty percent.
I mean, I could say that. I'd be lying, but I could say it.

title: Deep dive: offline sync, conflicts and idempotency
gist: Sam walks through a transactional outbox on SQLite, corrects themself that idempotency keys are generated on the client, explains moving from whole-record last-write-wins to per-field merges and intent-based money operations, and covers a queue that survives app kills with dead-lettering.

turns.t: Okay so let's go into the sync engine, because this is pretty close to stuff we deal with every day. Our drivers lose signal constantly, loading docks, parking garages, rural routes. Walk me through the architecture. Like, what's on the device, what happens when an agent hits save.

Sure. So on device we had SQLite, through WatermelonDB at first and later we moved to a thinner layer on top of op-sqlite because Watermelon's sync assumptions didn't fit us perfectly. When an agent does anything, say they record a repayment or they update a merchant's phone number, two things happen in one transaction. The local record gets updated, so the UI reflects it immediately, and we append an operation to an outbox table. The operation is like, type, entity id, the payload, a created-at, and an idempotency key. And the transaction matters, because if you update the record and then crash before writing the outbox entry, you've got a change that looks saved but never syncs. So it's both or neither.
Mm-hm.

Then there's a sync worker that drains the outbox. It sends operations in order per entity. It doesn't have to be globally ordered, but for a given merchant you want them in order, otherwise you get an update arriving before the create and the server's confused. When the server acks an operation, we mark it done and eventually delete it. And on the pull side, we kept a cursor, basically a server-side change sequence number, and the device asks for everything since its last cursor.
And the idempotency key, where does that come from?

So the server generates it when it first sees the request, and then — no, wait, sorry, that's backwards. That's completely backwards. The client generates it, at the moment the operation goes into the outbox. A UUID, v4 originally, later we used v7 because they sort by time, which was nice for debugging. It has to be the client, because the whole point is the case where the request reaches the server, the server applies it, and then the response gets lost because the agent walked into a basement. The client doesn't know if it worked, so it retries, and the retry has to carry the same key so the server can say, oh, I've seen this one, here's the original result. If the server generated the key, the retry would just look like a brand new request. Sorry, it's nine p.m., I'm going to blame the coffee.
No, that's good, you caught it. And how long does the server remember keys?

We kept them for seventy-two hours in a table keyed on device id plus the key. Which was based on, we looked at the longest realistic offline stretch, and agents in the field could go two days without signal, so seventy-two gave us a bit of margin. Beyond that, the operation itself had enough information that most things were naturally idempotent anyway, but not all of them.
Okay. Conflicts. Two agents edit the same merchant offline. What happens?

Yeah, so this is the bad call I mentioned. The first version was last write wins on the whole record. Each record had an updated-at, the later one wins, done. It's simple and it's easy to explain and it's wrong for us. Because what happened in practice is one agent updates the merchant's phone number in the morning, another agent, a different one, visits in the afternoon and updates the address, they both sync that night, and whoever syncs last overwrites the entire record. So you lose the phone number. And nobody notices until a collections call goes to the old number. We had, I think, a few hundred of those before we really understood the pattern.
Ouch.

Yeah. And also the timestamps were device clocks, so even 'later' was kind of a lie. One agent had their phone set to the wrong year. Literally the wrong year. So their writes won everything for about a week.
Oh no.

So we moved to per-field merges. Each field carries its own version, and the operation only sends the fields that actually changed, not the whole record. So phone and address don't conflict at all anymore, they're different fields, both changes survive. And for ordering we stopped trusting device clocks for conflict decisions, we used the server's sequence, so the version the client last saw. If you edit a field and the server's version of that field has moved since you last pulled, that's a real conflict, and then you need a policy.
And what was the policy?

Depends on the field, which is the honest answer. For most profile stuff, phone, address, opening hours, it's still last write wins but at the field level, by server arrival order, and we kept the losing value in a history table so support could recover it. For a few things we surfaced it to a human, like if two agents changed the merchant's legal name we flagged it for review instead of picking. And for money we just didn't do state merges at all.
Say more about that.

So the mistake you can make with money is syncing the balance. Like the client says, balance is now four hundred and fifty. If two agents both collect fifty euros offline from the same merchant, which did happen, family businesses, one cousin pays one agent and the other cousin pays the other, you end up with both clients saying balance is four-fifty and you've lost fifty euros. So instead the client never sends a balance. It sends an intent. Record payment of fifty euros, with the receipt number and the key. The server is the only thing that computes the balance, by applying the intents. Those commute, two payments of fifty is a hundred, order doesn't matter. The client shows a projected balance locally, with a little marker that says pending, but it's not authoritative.
Yeah. That's the right answer. We have the same split with stop status, kind of. Like 'mark delivered' is an event, not a field you overwrite.
Right, exactly. Events are so much easier to reason about than state when you're offline.

Okay, last piece, the queue surviving the app being killed. Because on Android especially, drivers swipe the app away, the OS kills it, the battery saver kills it. How did you make sure stuff actually got sent?

So the first principle is the outbox is on disk, in SQLite, so the app dying doesn't lose anything, it just delays it. Nothing is ever only in memory. The second part is getting it to actually flush. On Android we used WorkManager with a network-connected constraint, through a small native module, so when connectivity comes back the OS wakes us up even if the app's not running, and we run a headless JS task that drains the outbox. That was pretty reliable, except on some Xiaomi and Huawei phones with aggressive battery stuff, where we had to walk agents through whitelisting the app, which, not fun. On iOS it's worse, background fetch is basically whenever the OS feels like it, so we leaned on flushing whenever the app comes to the foreground, and on any network change while it's open. And we showed a count. Like 'three changes waiting to sync.' That turned out to matter a lot, actually, which is maybe a good segue for Priya.
Ha, hold that thought one sec. What about poison messages? Something the server rejects every single time.

Yeah, we had a retry policy with exponential backoff and jitter, and after a certain number of failures with a non-retryable error, like a validation error, a four-hundred class thing, we moved it to a dead-letter state. It stays on the device, it doesn't block the rest of the queue for other entities, and it shows up in a 'needs attention' list for the agent with a plain-language reason. The important thing was it didn't block other merchants' operations. Early on we had one bad operation that jammed the entire queue for an agent for two days. That's how we learned.
Everyone learns that one the hard way. How did you test any of this, by the way? Offline bugs are miserable to reproduce.

I think jamming the queue is mandatory, it's a rite of passage. Testing-wise, mostly by making the bad network reproducible on purpose. In dev builds we had a fake network layer with a little debug menu, so you could say drop every third request, or add four seconds of latency, or succeed on the server but lose the response, which is the nasty one. QA would run whole days in that mode. And on the server side we had a property-based test that took a random batch of operations, shuffled them, duplicated some, delivered them in different orders, and checked the final state always came out the same. That caught a lot of stuff we'd never have thought to write a test for. And honestly, a couple of us went out with agents once a quarter. Nothing replaces sitting in a car in the middle of nowhere with one bar, watching someone actually use the thing.

title: Working with design: pushing back with data
gist: Priya probes design collaboration; Sam tells how support-ticket data (30% of agent tickets were 'did it go through') led to a compromise sync indicator that cut those tickets about 40%, and how a designer rightly won an accessibility argument.

turns.t: Okay, Priya, you've been very patient.

No, this was great, honestly. So, my turn. On our side the driver app and the dashboard are pretty design-heavy, and I work really closely with the frontend engineers, like we pair a lot. So I'm curious how you've worked with designers. And maybe specifically, tell me about a time you disagreed with a design. What happened?

Yeah, okay, I have a good one, and it's actually related to the sync count thing. So when we did the offline rebuild, our designer at the time, Inês, she's great, she had this really strong principle that the agent shouldn't have to think about sync. Which I agree with, as a goal. And so her designs didn't show sync status anywhere. Things just saved, and the idea was the app would handle it invisibly, which is, you know, the dream.
Sure, that's very much the instinct.

And my gut said that's not going to work for these users, because they've been burned. They've had the old app eat their data. But a gut feeling isn't an argument, so instead of saying 'I think you're wrong,' I went and pulled support tickets from the previous quarter and tagged them. And roughly thirty percent of all tickets from field agents were some version of 'did my submission go through.' Not 'it failed,' just 'I don't know if it worked.' And then we had a handful of session recordings, with consent, where you could see agents submitting the same repayment two or three times because there was no feedback. Which, side note, is part of why idempotency mattered so much.
Right, right.

So I brought that to Inês, and I didn't bring a design, I just brought the data and said, here's the problem I think we're going to create. And she pushed back on some of it, which was fair, she said a big sync status bar would make agents anxious and they'd just stare at it all day. And she was right about that, actually. So we landed in the middle. A small indicator in the header, a little cloud icon with a number, that only shows up when there's something pending, and a sync history screen you can tap into if you care. And per item, like a little clock on a repayment that hasn't synced yet, which turns into a check.
And did it work? Did you measure it?

We did a quick test with five agents first, just in person at the office in Coimbra, before we built the full thing. And then after launch the 'did it go through' tickets dropped by, it was about forty percent over the next two months. Not to zero. Some people will always call. But the duplicate submissions mostly stopped.
That's a really nice story. I like that you brought the problem and not a solution.
I learned that the hard way too, honestly. Early in my career I'd show up with a Figma file I made myself and say, 'what about this,' and designers, quite reasonably, hated that.
Yeah, we do. A little.
Fair.
What about the other direction? Like when design pushed you on something you didn't want to do.

Oh, all the time. The one that comes to mind is accessibility. Inês pushed really hard for proper dynamic type support, because a lot of our agents were older and turned the font size way up on their phones. And I resisted, because our layouts were built with fixed heights everywhere and it was going to be a lot of work. And she just, she went and borrowed a phone from one of the agents with the font cranked all the way up, and showed me the app, and half the buttons were cut off. So, yeah. She won that one, rightly. That took us like three sprints.
That's the best way to win that argument.
It was very effective. I couldn't argue with the phone.
Last one from me, how do you like to work day to day with a designer? Like, when do you want to get pulled in?

Early, but not to make decisions. I like being in the room when the problem's being framed, mostly so I can say early, 'hey, this part's going to be expensive' or 'this part's basically free, we already have it.' Because designers don't always know what's cheap. And then I like a lot of small check-ins while building, rather than a big handoff and a big review. Like, I'll send a screen recording from a branch, 'here's how this transition feels on a real device,' because stuff that looks good in Figma can feel terrible on a five-year-old Android phone. Which is what most field workers have.
God, yes. Our drivers too. We test on a, I think it's a Galaxy A12, that's the baseline.
Exactly. That's the real target device.
